standard.title: Significant Events, Ideas and People in the Development of an Asian Society
standard.description: significant events, ideas, people, groups and/or movements in the development of an Asian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe how individuals and groups promote ideas and how significant events shape historical change (AC9HH9K18, AC9HH8K05, AC9HH8K10). They have not yet applied this analytical framework to the specific development of the chosen Asian society under European contact pressure.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe and explain significant events, ideas, people and movements in the development of the chosen Asian society — drawing from: the Boxer Rebellion and Chinese modernisation; Japan's Meiji Restoration period; or the Indian independence movement and key figures.

nodes.label: The central tension — tradition vs modernisation under colonial pressure
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the central tension facing Asian societies in this period — how to respond to European power while preserving cultural identity — and describe how this tension shaped significant events and movements.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain that Asian societies faced pressure to modernise (adopt European military and industrial methods) to resist European dominance, while also seeking to preserve their own cultural and political identity, and describe how this tension shaped at least one significant event or movement.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the core dilemma — adopt European methods and risk cultural transformation vs maintain tradition and risk military and economic subordination; examine how this tension produced different responses in different societies (China's Self-Strengthening Movement vs Japanese Meiji modernisation vs Indian nationalism); explain how the tension shaped the movements and figures in the following nodes.
wider: Examine whether this tradition/modernisation tension was unique to Asian societies under European pressure, or whether it reflects a universal pattern in how societies respond to powerful external challenges
nodes.hinge_reason: The tradition-vs-modernisation tension is the conceptual framework for understanding why specific figures and movements arose. Students who do not understand this tension cannot explain why the Boxer Rebellion and the Self-Strengthening Movement were both responses to the same pressure, or why the Meiji Restoration was so distinctive.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe individual events or figures without understanding the common structural tension driving them. Making the modernisation-tradition dilemma explicit is the scaffold for understanding why these specific figures and movements emerged when they did.

success_criteria: Explains the tension between modernisation and cultural preservation in the chosen Asian society
Describes how this tension shaped at least one significant event or movement

nodes.label: Significant events, individuals and movements in the chosen society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe significant events, individuals, groups and movements in the development of the chosen Asian society, explaining the role each played and what it achieved.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two significant individuals or events from the chosen society and explain the role each played in the society's development.
nodes.typical_width: For China: the Self-Strengthening Movement, Christian missionaries, Empress Dowager Cixi, the Boxer Rebellion and Society of Righteous Harmony; for Japan: Emperor Mutsuhito (Meiji), Commodore Perry's arrival, the Satsuma Rebellion, samurai resistance to modernisation; for India: the British East India Company, the Sepoy Rebellion, Indian National Congress, Gokhale, Naoroji, Tilak, early Gandhi; for Indonesia: Diponegoro, Java War, Budi Utomo, Sarekat Islam, Sukarno, Hatta, Sjahrir; describe what each figure or movement sought to achieve, what strategies they used, and what they accomplished.
wider: Examine the Boxer Rebellion (or equivalent chosen society event) from both Chinese and European perspectives — analysing how the same events were understood and justified differently
Investigate a figure from the chosen society in depth — examining their motivations, strategies, achievements and legacy
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multi-perspective analysis of events like the Boxer Rebellion — or the Sepoy Rebellion, or Satsuma Rebellion — produces genuine historical complexity where students must navigate conflicting accounts and evaluations. Individual investigations build depth within the chosen society's narrative.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly focus on the most dramatic or well-known event or figure without building a picture of the range of responses — from accommodation to resistance to modernisation — that characterised the chosen society's development.

success_criteria: Describes at least two significant individuals or events in the chosen society's development
Explains the role each played and what it achieved or failed to achieve
